blocks.text: Now, the same objection could be raised regarding the doves of Semiramis. For although the later Syrians also worshipped יונים jonim, that is, domestic doves, those properly so called, out of regard for Semiramis, it nevertheless seems possible to infer, even from Ctesias, that wild doves were attendant on her. For he calls the places in which those doves lived desert and rocky, ἐρήμους, καὶ πετρώδεις τόπους [erēmous, kai petrōdeis topous]. Accordingly the name of Semiramis, taken from this, is explained by Hesychius as περιστερὰ ὄρειος [peristera oreios], mountain dove. We have shown elsewhere that this word is Arabic, not Syrian as is supposed, and that it was written Serimam, which the Greeks changed διὰ τὴν εὐφωνίαν [dia tēn euphōnian] into Σεμίραμιν [Semiramin]. For among the Arabs حمام [ḥmām] himam is dove, and سراة [srāh] sera mountain, شعرا [shʿrā] sera forest, صحرا [ṣḥrā] sahra desert; from some one of these words joined with حمام [ḥmām] himam the name Serimam was formed, for dove of the mountain, or of the forest, or of the desert. Such is the composition in the words כרמיון charmion or כרמיונא charmiona, of which we have spoken, and חריונים chirjonim or דביונים dibjonim, of [II, 532] which we shall speak. But the chief point is this: from the history of Semiramis it can in no way be proved that doves were already worshipped in Syria in ancient times, because her date is quite uncertain. For if we follow Ctesias, a highly fabulous writer, Semiramis was the wife of Ninus, whose reign would fall in the times of Abraham. But others make Semiramis the daughter of Belochus, who was more than five hundred years later than Ninus. Hence Eusebius at the number 582, which is the tenth year from the death of Joshua: Eighteenth king of the Assyrians, Belochus, for 25 years; whose daughter Atossa, who is also Semiramis, reigned with her father for 12 years. And Photius, on author 186, concerning the Canon, Hist. 9: Ὅσα οἱ ἄλλοι περὶ Ἀττόσης Ἀσσυρίου ἀναγράφουσι, ταῦθ᾽ οὗτος εἰς Σεμίραμιν ἀναφέρει· [Hosa hoi alloi peri Attosēs Assyriou anagraphousi, tauth᾽ houtos eis Semiramin anapherei] Whatever others write about Atossa the Assyrian, he refers to Semiramis. But, what is more surprising, if we believe Herodotus in his first book, Semiramis was older only by πέντε γενεαῖς [pente geneais], five generations, that is, at most two hundred years, than Nitocris, the mother of that Labonitus whom Cyrus defeated. Yet between Cyrus and Belochus more than a thousand years intervene, and between him and Ninus fifteen or sixteen hundred. Nor can the deeds of Semiramis be referred to the age of Abraham, when, as may be gathered from Gen. XIV, the king of שנער, or Babylonia, was a petty prince. And equally uncertain is what some assert, that the kings of Babylonia had the dove [col. 8] as a military standard, since no ancient author is cited who reports this ^{(2)}. And it is most probable that Cyrus, after subjecting the Babylonians to his rule, adopted the same military standards that his predecessors, the Medes and Assyrians, had had. But that he had an eagle as his standard is clear from these words of Xenophon in the seventh book of the Cyropaedia: Ἦν δ᾽ αὐτῷ τὸ σημεῖον ἀετὸς χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ δόρατος μακροῦ ἀνατεταμένος [Ēn d᾽ autō to sēmeion aetos chrysous epi doratos makrou anatetamenos]. His standard was a golden eagle, stretched out upon a long spear. This all the kings of the Persians thereafter imitated. The same Xenophon: Καὶ νῦν δὲ ἔτι τοῦτο τὸ σημεῖον τῷ Περσῶν βασιλεῖ διαμένει· [Kai nyn de eti touto to sēmeion tō Persōn basilei diamenei] This standard still remains even today for the king of the Persians. Curtius, book 3, on the army of Darius: Among these they had consecrated a golden eagle, resembling one spreading its wings. Philostratus in the Heroica, in the chapter on Themistocles: Μῆδοι ταῦτα, καὶ Βαβυλὼν μέση, καὶ τὸ σημεῖον τὸ βασίλειον ὁ χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ τῆς πέλτης ἀετός· [Mēdoi tauta, kai Babylōn mesē, kai to sēmeion to basileion ho chrysous epi tēs peltēs aetos] These things are the Medes, and Babylon in the middle, and the military standard, a golden eagle upon a spear. Therefore in Jeremiah [XXV, 38. XLVI,16. L,16.] חרב היונה is not, as I at least think, the sword of the dove, but the oppressing or devastating sword, such as that of the Babylonians was under King Nebuchadnezzar ^{(3)}. Accordingly [II, 533] the prophet says of the same, Ierem. XLVI, 14: אכלה חרב סביביך, The sword has devoured round about you. But that the Samaritans also worshipped doves is entirely fabulous. What idols they worshipped when they were first transplanted from Assyria into Samaria is related in 2 Reg. XVII, 30. 31.: The men of Babylon made Succoth-Benoth, the Cuthites made Nergal, etc. But there the Sacred History says not a γρῦ [gry] about a dove, or its image, worshipped by them. Nor was this anywhere charged against them by Josephus, who in many places inveighs sharply against them. See the ninth book of the Jewish Antiquities, and the end of the eleventh; and chapters 1 and 7 of book 12; and chapter 6 of book 13; and chapters 3 and 5 of book 18; and chapter 5 of book 20. Nor could the worship of the dove, or of its image, in any way have been consistent with the Law of Moses, which they accepted. For, to say nothing of the fact that all images are forbidden so often and so expressly by Moses, on what pretext could they possibly have worshipped the very animal which they were commanded to slaughter to God in sacrifice? Nevertheless it is undoubtedly true, as Xenophon, Ctesias, Lucian and other eyewitnesses, αὐτόπται [autoptai], assert, that the Syrians and Assyrians either worshipped doves as goddesses, or at least abstained from them as from something sacred. But at what precise time this superstition was introduced into Syria or Assyria, no one could easily say.
